en.title: Public Health: the whole course
en.short: What public health is, how the degree is organised, its main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These notes teach public health concepts to students. They are not medical advice, and they do not give drug doses or treatment protocols. Clinical and programme guidelines change often and differ between countries, so check the current national ministry of health or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance before you act on any detail.

Public health decisions affect whole populations, so the notes stress evidence, ethics and local context. Where a rule or qualification belongs to one country, it is named. Anyone who is unwell should seek local medical help.

sections.heading: What public health is
sections.text:
Public health is the organised effort to protect and improve the health of populations rather than of one patient at a time. It asks who is getting sick, where, when and why, and then acts on the answers through prevention, policy and services.

Its core functions are often described as assessment of health needs, policy development, and assurance that services are delivered. It draws on epidemiology, biostatistics, social sciences, environmental health, economics, law and management. A public health worker may never treat an individual patient, but must still understand clinical care well enough to plan and evaluate it.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
Length, awards and entry routes differ by country and institution, so check your own student handbook. In Nigeria, public health is often studied at postgraduate level, for example a Master of Public Health (MPH) after a first degree in medicine, nursing, pharmacy, environmental health or a social science. Some universities also offer a BSc in Public Health. Community medicine is taught within the MBBS programme.

In the United Kingdom, both BSc and MPH routes exist, and the Faculty of Public Health sets training standards for specialist registration. In the United States, the MPH is common and the DrPH is a doctoral route. Many programmes are taught, some are research based, and some are distance learning.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics come first: concepts and history, determinants and inequity, demography, health indicators, biostatistics, epidemiology, environmental health, health promotion, and health systems with primary health care. These give the vocabulary and the measuring tools for everything later.

Core topics apply that base: study designs and causal inference, surveillance and outbreak investigation, applied data analysis, screening and diagnostic tests, communicable disease control, immunisation, maternal, newborn and child health, nutrition and food safety, noncommunicable diseases, occupational health, water, sanitation and hygiene, policy and planning, economics and financing, ethics and law, health information and monitoring and evaluation, community diagnosis, and emergency preparedness.

Master’s level work adds advanced epidemiological methods, implementation science and evaluation, planetary health and climate change, and research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn each measure by using it. Calculate a rate, an odds ratio or a sensitivity from a small table, then explain what the number means in plain words. Link every topic to a real programme you know, such as an immunisation campaign or a village water project.

Practise interpreting graphs, tables and study abstracts. Write short answers to questions such as: what is the denominator, what is the comparison group, and what would change the conclusion? Space your revision and test yourself rather than only rereading. For the dissertation, choose a question early and read widely before collecting data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students confuse incidence with prevalence, or a rate with a count, and then draw the wrong conclusion. Others describe a disease in detail but forget the population, the setting and the comparison group.

A common error is to quote one country’s guideline or law as if it were universal. Another is to propose a programme without a budget, an indicator or an evaluation plan. In ethics and outbreak work, students sometimes ignore consent, stigma and the duty to protect confidentiality. Finally, do not treat notes such as these as clinical advice.

keyPoints: Public health protects and improves the health of populations, not only of individual patients.
Its core functions are assessment, policy development and assurance of services.
Degrees, entry routes and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Epidemiology and biostatistics are the basic measuring tools of the subject.
Learn measures by calculating them and explaining what the result means.
Guidelines and laws differ between countries and change, so check the current official source.

en.title: Public health: concepts, core functions and history
en.short: What public health is, its three core functions, and its history from sanitary reform to Alma-Ata.

sections.heading: Defining public health
sections.text:
Public health is the organised effort to prevent disease, prolong life and promote health across whole populations. C-E A Winslow’s 1920 definition is still quoted. The focus is the group, not the individual.

Clinical medicine asks what is wrong with this person and how to treat it. Public health asks why this group is sick, and acts upstream: safe water, clean air, food safety, vaccination, housing, law and health education. It draws on epidemiology, biostatistics and social sciences.

sections.heading: The core functions
sections.text:
The US Institute of Medicine named three core functions in 1988; they remain a common framework.

Assessment: measure the health of the population, using births, deaths, surveys and surveillance, and identify unmet needs.

Policy development: turn that evidence into priorities, plans, laws and budgets, with communities and other sectors.

Assurance: make sure services exist, are reachable and are of good quality; enforce public health law; evaluate results.

sections.heading: Sanitary reform and cholera
sections.text:
Sanitary reform in nineteenth-century Britain linked dirt and overcrowding to disease. Edwin Chadwick’s 1842 report led to the Public Health Act 1848, which set up a General Board of Health. The theory behind it was miasma, bad air, yet drains and clean water helped.

In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho, London, and traced them to the Broad Street water pump, evidence that cholera travels in water. The pump handle story is often embellished; the mapping and investigation are documented.

Pasteur and Koch established germ theory in the 1870s and 1880s.

sections.heading: Global and African milestones
sections.text:
Alma-Ata (WHO and UNICEF, 1978) called for Health for All by the year 2000 through primary health care. The Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986) set out health promotion: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reoriented services.

African milestones include Tanzania’s 1973 Mtu ni Afya health campaign, the 2001 Abuja Declaration on health financing, adopted by the Organisation of African Unity (now the African Union), and the 2008 Ouagadougou Declaration on primary health care and health systems in Africa. The 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa showed why surveillance and strong systems matter.

keyPoints: Public health works on populations and prevention; clinical medicine treats individual patients.
The three core functions are assessment, policy development and assurance (US Institute of Medicine, 1988).
Sanitary reform and John Snow’s 1854 cholera mapping showed that water supply and environment shape disease.
Germ theory gave public health a specific target: the micro-organism.
Alma-Ata 1978 made primary health care the route to Health for All; the Ottawa Charter 1986 broadened this to health promotion.
African milestones include the Abuja Declaration 2001 and the Ouagadougou Declaration 2008.

en.title: Determinants of health and health inequity
en.short: Biological, social, economic and political influences on health, and how inequities are measured.

sections.heading: Determinants of health
sections.text: Health is shaped by many factors, not only medical care. Biological determinants include age, sex and inherited traits. Behavioural determinants include smoking, diet, physical activity and alcohol use. Social determinants include education, occupation, social support and discrimination. Economic determinants include income, wealth and employment. Environmental determinants include air and water quality, housing and climate. Political determinants include laws, taxation, governance and the distribution of power and resources. These factors interact; low income, for example, can limit healthy food and safe housing.

sections.heading: Layers of influence
sections.text: Dahlgren and Whitehead picture these influences as layers. At the centre are individual factors such as age, sex and constitutional make-up. Around them are individual lifestyle factors. Next are social and community networks. Then living and working conditions, including education, work, water and sanitation, and health services. The outer layer is general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions. Changing only individual behaviour misses the conditions that shape it.

sections.heading: Equality and equity
sections.text: Equality means giving everyone the same. Equity means giving people what they need to reach good health, which may require different support. A health inequality is any observed difference in health between groups. A health inequity is a difference that is avoidable, unfair and unjust. The social gradient describes a stepwise pattern: health tends to be worse at each lower level of income, education or occupation, not only among the poorest. This points to unequal living and working conditions.

sections.heading: Measuring inequity
sections.text: Health inequalities are measured by comparing rates between groups. The absolute difference is one rate minus another. The relative difference is a ratio, such as a rate ratio. Example: if a disease rate is 20 per 1,000 in a low-income group and 10 per 1,000 in a high-income group, the absolute difference is 10 per 1,000 and the rate ratio is 2.0. Both matter: the absolute difference shows the burden; the ratio shows how many times higher. Check data quality, group size and whether the difference is avoidable.

keyPoints: Determinants include biological, behavioural, social, economic, environmental and political factors that interact.
Dahlgren and Whitehead’s layers run from individual factors to lifestyle, networks, living and working conditions, and general socioeconomic conditions.
Equality gives everyone the same; equity gives different support according to need.
A health inequality is an observed difference; a health inequity is avoidable, unfair and unjust.
The social gradient means health worsens stepwise with lower socioeconomic position, not only at the poorest level.
Absolute difference = rate in group A − rate in group B; rate ratio = rate in group A ÷ rate in group B, and both should be interpreted with data quality in mind.

en.title: Demography and population health
en.short: Population data sources, fertility and mortality measures, age structure and the demographic transition.

sections.heading: Sources of population data
sections.text:
A census counts everyone in a country at one time. It is the most complete source, but it is costly, usually held every ten years, and goes out of date. Vital registration records births and deaths as they happen; it is complete only where most events are registered. Sample surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Surveys, ask a sample of households about fertility, child mortality and health.

All three have errors: undercounting, late registration and sampling error. Compare sources before trusting a figure, and note the year.

sections.heading: Fertility and mortality
sections.text:
Fertility means actual births; fecundity is the biological ability to conceive. The crude birth rate is births in a year divided by the mid-year population, times 1,000. Example: 1,200 births in a population of 40,000 gives 1,200 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000.

The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. Mortality measures include the crude death rate, the infant mortality rate (deaths under one year per 1,000 live births) and life expectancy at birth.

sections.heading: Age structure and dependency
sections.text:
A population pyramid plots age groups against numbers, separately for males and females. A wide base means high fertility; a narrow base means falling fertility. The dependency ratio compares people likely to depend on others with those of working age, usually 15 to 64.

Example: 420 aged 0 to 14, 540 aged 15 to 64, 40 aged 65 and over.
Child dependency = 420 ÷ 540 × 100 = 77.8
Old-age dependency = 40 ÷ 540 × 100 = 7.4
Total = 85.2 dependants per 100 working-age people.

sections.heading: Transition and planning
sections.text: The demographic transition is the shift from high birth and death rates, through falling death rates and rapid growth, to low birth and death rates. Countries with high fertility need more maternal and child health services; ageing countries need more care for chronic disease. Migration also changes demand. Check current census and WHO data.

keyPoints: Censuses, vital registration and sample surveys are the main population data sources, each with errors.
Crude birth rate = births in a year ÷ mid-year population × 1,000.
Total fertility rate estimates lifetime births per woman at current rates.
Infant mortality rate = deaths under one year ÷ live births × 1,000.
Dependency ratio = dependants ÷ working-age population × 100.
The demographic transition links falling fertility and mortality to changing health service needs.

en.title: Health indicators and the measurement of disease
en.short: Rates, incidence and prevalence, standardisation, mortality indicators, life expectancy, DALYs and data limits.

sections.heading: Rates and denominators
sections.text:
A ratio compares two quantities, such as men to women. A proportion is a ratio where the numerator is part of the denominator, so it ranges from 0 to 1 and is often shown as a percentage. A rate measures events per unit of population per unit of time. The denominator is the population at risk. If the denominator is wrong, the indicator is wrong.

Example: 300 new cases in 100,000 people at risk in one year gives 300 ÷ 100,000 = 0.003, or 300 per 100,000 person-years.

sections.heading: Incidence and prevalence
sections.text: Incidence is the number of new cases in a defined period divided by the population at risk at the start. Prevalence is the number of existing cases at a point or period divided by the total population. Incidence measures risk of becoming ill; prevalence measures burden. For a stable condition, prevalence is roughly incidence × average duration. A long-lasting disease can have high prevalence even with low incidence.

sections.heading: Mortality and standardisation
sections.text: Crude rates use the whole population. Specific rates use a subgroup, such as age or sex. Standardised rates adjust for differences in age structure, using direct or indirect methods, so groups can be compared fairly. Infant mortality rate is deaths under age 1 per 1,000 live births in a year. Under-five mortality rate is deaths under age 5 per 1,000 live births. Maternal mortality ratio is maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. These differ by country and year; check current national or WHO data.

sections.heading: Life expectancy and DALYs
sections.text: Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if current age-specific death rates stayed constant. A disability-adjusted life year (DALY) is one lost year of healthy life. It adds years of life lost to premature death (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD). Routine data have limits: incomplete birth and death registration, misclassified causes, and uncertain denominators. Facility data miss people who never attend. Always ask who is counted and who is missing.

keyPoints: A proportion is a part over the whole; a rate adds a time dimension and uses the population at risk as denominator.
Incidence = new cases ÷ population at risk over a period; prevalence = existing cases ÷ total population.
For a stable condition, prevalence is roughly incidence × average duration.
Crude rates describe whole populations; specific rates describe subgroups; standardised rates adjust for age structure.

Infant mortality uses deaths under age 1 per 1,000 live births; under-five mortality uses deaths under age 5 per 1,000 live births; maternal mortality ratio uses maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
Life expectancy at birth uses current age-specific death rates, DALY = YLL + YLD, and routine data are limited by incomplete registration and uncertain denominators.

en.title: Foundations of biostatistics
en.short: Covers data types, distributions, sampling error, confidence intervals, p-values and power.

sections.heading: Data and description
sections.text: Data are observations recorded as numbers or categories. Categorical data fall into groups. Numerical data are discrete, such as counts, or continuous, such as blood pressure. Descriptive summaries describe a sample without generalising. For categorical data use counts and proportions. For numerical data use the mean and standard deviation when the shape is roughly symmetric, or the median and interquartile range, the spread of the middle half, when skewed. The mean is Σx ÷ n. The standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.

sections.heading: Probability and distributions
sections.text: Probability is the long-run chance of an event, from 0 to 1. The normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve defined by its mean and standard deviation; about 95% of values lie within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. The binomial distribution gives the probability of r successes in n independent trials, each with the same success probability p. It applies to yes or no outcomes.

sections.heading: Sampling and confidence
sections.text: A sample is a subset of a population. Random sampling reduces bias, but estimates vary between samples. Sampling error is this natural variation. The standard error of a mean is SE = s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. A 95% confidence interval, a range of plausible population values, is roughly estimate ± 1.96 × SE. Example: mean 120, s = 10, n = 100. SE = 10 ÷ √100 = 1. The interval is 120 ± 1.96, or 118.04 to 121.96.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.text: A hypothesis test compares data with a null hypothesis, usually no difference. The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true. A significance level, often 0.05, is chosen before the test. A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis; a type II error fails to reject a false one. Power is the chance of detecting a real difference, often 80% or more.

keyPoints: Data are categorical or numerical; summarise categorical data with counts and proportions, and numerical data with mean and standard deviation or median and interquartile range.
Mean = Σx ÷ n, and the standard error of a mean is SE = s ÷ √n.

The normal distribution is symmetric, with about 95% of values within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean; the binomial distribution models successes in independent trials with the same probability p.
A 95% confidence interval is roughly estimate ± 1.96 × SE.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null is true.
A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis, a type II error fails to reject a false one, and power is the chance of detecting a real difference.

en.title: Foundations of epidemiology
en.short: Definition, uses, natural history, prevention levels, frequency and association measures, designs, bias and causation.

sections.heading: Definition and uses
sections.text: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants (causes and risk factors) of health-related states in populations and applies the findings to control health problems. It works at population level, not just with individual patients. It is used to describe disease burden, identify risk factors, evaluate interventions and guide policy. Disease varies by person, place and time.

sections.heading: Natural history and prevention
sections.text: The natural history of disease is its course from exposure to outcome without treatment. It moves through susceptibility, presymptomatic change, clinical disease and then recovery, disability or death. Primary prevention stops disease before it starts, for example immunisation or safe water. Secondary prevention detects disease early, such as screening. Tertiary prevention limits disability after disease, such as rehabilitation. Primordial prevention addresses underlying social and environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Frequency and association
sections.text: Incidence is the number of new cases in a population over a period. Prevalence is the number of existing cases at a point or period. Risk is the proportion who develop disease. The risk ratio (RR) compares risk in exposed and unexposed groups: RR = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed. The odds ratio (OR) compares odds of exposure in cases and controls: OR = odds in cases ÷ odds in controls. Example: in a cohort of 100 exposed and 100 unexposed people, 20 exposed and 10 unexposed develop disease. Risk exposed = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20. Risk unexposed = 10 ÷ 100 = 0.10. RR = 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 2.0. Exposed people had twice the risk.

sections.heading: Designs, bias and causation
sections.text: Descriptive studies describe patterns by person, place and time; examples are case reports and cross-sectional surveys. Analytical studies test associations; cohort studies follow people over time, case-control studies compare past exposures, and trials test interventions. Bias is systematic error. Selection bias comes from how people enter a study. Information bias comes from faulty measurement. Confounding occurs when another factor is linked to both exposure and outcome. Association is not causation; consider temporality, consistency, dose-response and plausibility.

keyPoints: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health states in populations.
Natural history runs from susceptibility to outcome; primary, secondary and tertiary prevention act at different stages.
Incidence counts new cases; prevalence counts existing cases.
Risk ratio = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; odds ratio = odds of exposure in cases ÷ odds of exposure in controls.
In the worked cohort, RR = 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 2.0.
Descriptive studies describe patterns; analytical studies test associations, but bias and confounding must be considered before inferring causation.

en.title: Foundations of environmental health
en.short: Hazards in air, water, soil, food and housing, and how to assess and control them.

sections.heading: Hazards and pathways
sections.text: Environmental health studies how surroundings affect health. A hazard is anything that can cause harm. Physical hazards include noise, heat, radiation and injury risks. Chemical hazards include lead, arsenic, pesticides and air pollutants. Biological hazards include bacteria, viruses, parasites and moulds. They reach people through air, water, soil, food and housing. An exposure pathway links a source, such as a polluted well, to a route, such as drinking, and to a person. Housing matters: crowding, damp, poor ventilation and unsafe cooking fuels increase exposure.

sections.heading: Water, sanitation, vectors
sections.text: Water supply, sanitation, vector control and waste management are core controls. Safe water means protecting the source, treating it and keeping it clean to the point of use. Sanitation separates human waste from people, water and food. Vectors are organisms that carry disease, such as mosquitoes, flies and rodents. Vector control removes breeding sites and reduces contact. Waste management collects and disposes of solid, liquid and hazardous waste safely. Climate effects include heatwaves, floods, droughts and changing vector ranges; these can contaminate water, damage crops and displace people.

sections.heading: Risk assessment and control
sections.text: Risk assessment has four steps: hazard identification, dose-response assessment, exposure assessment and risk characterisation. Hazard is the potential to cause harm; risk is the chance of harm under actual conditions. Control follows a hierarchy: remove the hazard, substitute something safer, use engineering controls, then administrative controls, and finally personal protective equipment. For example, a child drinks 1 litre of water a day containing 5 micrograms of a chemical per litre. Daily intake is 1 × 5 = 5 micrograms. Compare this with the current World Health Organization (WHO) or national guideline; do not set your own safe level. Guidelines differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Environmental health links hazards in air, water, soil, food and housing to exposure and disease.
Physical, chemical and biological hazards reach people by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact.
Safe water, sanitation, vector control and waste management are core environmental controls.
Risk assessment has four steps: hazard identification, dose-response, exposure assessment and risk characterisation.
Control follows a hierarchy, from removing the hazard to personal protective equipment.
Daily intake = concentration × amount consumed per day; compare with current official guidelines.

en.title: Health promotion and health education
en.short: Ottawa Charter action areas, prevention and protection, behaviour change models and low-literacy education.

sections.heading: Promotion, prevention, protection
sections.text: Health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over their health. The Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986) names five action areas: build healthy public policy, create supportive environments, strengthen community action, develop personal skills and reorient health services. Health education is planned learning that improves health literacy, the ability to find, understand and use health information; it is one part of promotion. Disease prevention aims to stop disease before it starts (primary), find it early (secondary) or limit disability (tertiary). Health protection uses laws, regulation and services, such as clean water and outbreak control, to reduce hazards.

sections.heading: Behaviour change models
sections.text: Behaviour change models help explain why people act. The health belief model says action is more likely when a person feels susceptible, believes the condition is serious, sees benefits outweigh barriers, and gets a cue to act; self-efficacy (confidence to act) was added later. The stages of change model describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, so support should match the stage. Social cognitive theory stresses that people learn by observing others, that personal, behavioural and environmental factors interact, and that self-efficacy and reinforcement shape action.

sections.heading: Low-literacy education
sections.text: Education for low-literacy audiences uses plain language, short sentences, pictures and the local language. Avoid jargon, teach one or two actions at a time, and check understanding with teach-back: the learner explains or shows the step in their own words. In a market in Kano, Nigeria, a health worker named Amina teaches handwashing. She uses a six-picture poster, speaks Hausa, demonstrates, and asks each trader to show the steps back. She says germs from the toilet can reach the mouth, instead of using the term faecal-oral. This respects the audience and makes the message usable.

keyPoints: Health promotion enables people to improve control over health; health education is one part of it.
The Ottawa Charter action areas are healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reoriented health services.
Disease prevention works at primary, secondary and tertiary levels; health protection uses regulation and services to reduce hazards.
The health belief model weighs perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers and cues to action.
Stages of change matches support to readiness; social cognitive theory stresses observation, self-efficacy and environment.
For low-literacy audiences use plain language, pictures, local language and teach-back.

en.title: Health systems and primary health care
en.short: WHO building blocks, levels of care, primary health care, financing models and how UHC is measured.

sections.heading: Building blocks
sections.text:
A health system is all the people, institutions and actions whose main aim is to promote, restore or maintain health. The World Health Organization (WHO) names six building blocks: service delivery; health workforce; health information systems; medical products, vaccines and technologies; health financing; and leadership and governance. They are interdependent; weak supplies or unmotivated staff undermine good services.

The blocks are a planning framework; countries organise them differently.

sections.heading: Levels of care
sections.text:
Care is arranged in levels. Community care is close to homes, through community health workers. Primary care is first contact with the formal system, such as a health centre. Secondary care is specialist care, at a district hospital. Tertiary care is highly specialised, such as a teaching or referral hospital.

The district health system is the local system for a defined district. It links community services, primary care facilities and a district hospital through referral. Names and boundaries vary by country.

Case: a community health worker refers a child with fast breathing to the health centre. The centre stabilises and refers to the district hospital.

sections.heading: Primary health care
sections.text:
Primary health care (PHC) is a whole-system approach, not only first-contact clinics. The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 set principles: equity; community participation; intersectoral collaboration, meaning action with sectors such as education and water; appropriate technology; and prevention alongside treatment. PHC should be accessible, affordable, comprehensive and continuous.

PHC differs from primary care. Primary care is the first clinical service; PHC adds community action and action on wider causes of ill health.

sections.heading: Financing and UHC
sections.text:
Health financing models include tax funding, social health insurance, private insurance, out-of-pocket payments and community schemes. Many countries mix them. Tax funding pools risk widely; social insurance links contributions to entitlement; out-of-pocket payment can push people into poverty.

Universal health coverage (UHC) means all people receive needed health services without financial hardship. It is measured with a service coverage index and financial protection indicators, especially catastrophic out-of-pocket spending, meaning health costs above a set share of household spending, and impoverishing spending, which pushes households into poverty. Check current WHO and World Bank sources.

keyPoints: WHO’s six building blocks are service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, medical products, health financing, and leadership and governance.
Care is organised from community and primary levels to secondary and tertiary levels, linked by referral.
The district health system is the local system for a defined district, usually linking community services, primary care and a district hospital.
Primary health care is a whole-system approach based on equity, community participation, intersectoral action, appropriate technology and prevention.
Health financing may combine tax funding, social health insurance, private insurance, out-of-pocket payments and community schemes.
Universal health coverage means needed services without financial hardship, measured by service coverage and financial protection indicators.

en.title: Epidemiological study designs and causal inference
en.short: Cross-sectional, case-control, cohort and randomised studies; bias, confounding and causal judgement.

sections.heading: Main designs
sections.text: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time. They describe prevalence but cannot establish time order. Case-control studies start with people who have an outcome (cases) and compare their past exposure with controls. They suit rare outcomes but are prone to recall bias. Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed people forward and measure incidence; they can show time order. Randomised controlled trials allocate participants by chance, so known and unknown confounders tend to balance between groups; they give the strongest evidence for causation when well conducted.

sections.heading: Bias and confounding
sections.text: Selection bias occurs when the groups compared are not representative or are chosen differently. Information bias occurs when exposure or outcome is measured wrongly, including recall bias. Confounding is a third factor, linked to both exposure and outcome but not part of the causal pathway, that distorts their apparent relation. For example, in a cohort, 30 of 100 exposed and 10 of 100 unexposed develop disease. Risk ratio = (30÷100) ÷ (10÷100) = 3.0. If the exposed group is older and age raises risk, age is a confounder.

sections.heading: Control and effect modification
sections.text: Matching chooses controls or comparison groups similar to cases or exposed people on confounders. Stratification analyses the association within levels of a confounder, such as age groups. Adjustment uses statistical models to estimate the association while holding measured confounders constant. These methods control only measured confounders. Effect modification means the size of an association differs across groups, for example by sex; it is a finding to report, not a nuisance to remove.

sections.heading: Judging causation
sections.text: Bradford Hill viewpoints help judge whether an association is causal: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. They are viewpoints, not a checklist, and none is sufficient alone. Temporality, exposure before outcome, is essential. Judgement also considers bias, confounding and study quality. Guidelines and policy should cite current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Cross-sectional studies measure prevalence at one time; case-control studies compare past exposure in cases and controls; cohort studies measure incidence forward in time.
For a 2×2 table with exposed cases a, exposed non-cases b, unexposed cases c and unexposed non-cases d, risk ratio = [a ÷ (a+b)] ÷ [c ÷ (c+d)] and odds ratio = (a × d) ÷ (b × c).
Randomisation tends to balance known and unknown confounders, so a well-conducted randomised trial gives the strongest evidence for causation.
Selection bias, information bias and confounding are the main threats to valid comparison.
Matching, stratification and statistical adjustment control measured confounders, not unmeasured ones.
Bradford Hill viewpoints guide causal judgement, but temporality is essential and no single viewpoint proves causation.

en.title: Disease surveillance and outbreak investigation
en.short: Surveillance types, notifiable reporting, IHR, outbreak steps, epidemic curves and after-action review.

sections.heading: Surveillance systems
sections.text: Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, shared with people who need it for action. Passive surveillance relies on routine reports from health facilities; it is cheap but incomplete. Active surveillance means staff search for cases, for example by visiting clinics or households. Sentinel surveillance uses selected sites, such as a few hospitals, to give early warning or monitor trends. Syndromic surveillance counts symptom patterns, such as fever with rash, before laboratory confirmation. Each method trades completeness against speed and cost.

sections.heading: Reporting and IHR
sections.text: Notifiable disease reporting requires clinicians and laboratories to report listed diseases to the public health authority. The list differs by country and changes, so check current national guidance. Under the International Health Regulations (2005), WHO member states must develop core surveillance and response capacities and notify WHO of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. Each state names a national focal point for this communication.

sections.heading: Outbreak investigation
sections.text: An outbreak is more cases of a disease than expected in a place and time. The steps are: confirm the outbreak exists; verify the diagnosis; define a case; find cases; describe them by time, place and person; form hypotheses; test them; control the source; communicate; and write a report. The epidemic curve plots cases by date of onset. A single sharp peak suggests a point source. A rising and falling curve with successive peaks suggests person-to-person spread. Attack rate = cases ÷ people at risk × 100. If 18 of 30 funeral guests become ill, the attack rate is 18 ÷ 30 × 100 = 60%.

sections.heading: Risk assessment and review
sections.text: Rapid risk assessment is a structured judgement of the hazard, exposure, context, vulnerability and response capacity, including uncertainty, to guide action. After-action review is a structured review after the event of what worked, what failed and what should change. It should be blameless and lead to recommendations with owners and dates.

keyPoints: Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and sharing of health data for action.
Passive surveillance uses routine reports; active searches for cases; sentinel uses selected sites; syndromic uses symptom patterns.
Notifiable disease lists differ by country; under the International Health Regulations (2005), states must notify WHO of events that may be a public health emergency of international concern.
Outbreak steps include confirming the outbreak, defining a case, finding cases, describing time place and person, testing hypotheses, control, communication and a report.
An epidemic curve plots cases by date of onset; a point source gives one peak, while person-to-person spread gives successive peaks.
Attack rate = cases ÷ people at risk × 100; rapid risk assessment guides response, and after-action review identifies lessons.

en.title: Applied biostatistics and data analysis
en.short: Choosing and interpreting tests, regression, survival analysis, missing data and honest reporting.

sections.heading: Choosing tests
sections.text:
Choose a test from the question, outcome type and design. For two independent means, use an independent t-test when the outcome is roughly normal; for paired means, use a paired t-test. For three or more means, use ANOVA. For two categorical variables, use chi-square; for paired binary data, use McNemar. Report the effect size and a 95% confidence interval, not only a p-value. A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability that the null is true.

Example: group A mean systolic pressure 130 mmHg (SD 10, n=10); group B 124 mmHg (SD 10, n=10). Pooled SD 10. Standard error of difference = √(100/10 + 100/10) = 4.47. t = (130 − 124)/4.47 = 1.34, df = 18. Two-sided p ≈ 0.20. There is no clear evidence of a difference.

sections.heading: Association and prediction
sections.text: Correlation measures the strength of a straight-line relationship between two continuous variables. Pearson correlation assumes roughly normal data; Spearman correlation uses ranks. Correlation does not prove causation. Linear regression models a continuous outcome: y = a + bx. The slope b is the mean change in y per one-unit increase in x. Logistic regression models a binary outcome and reports odds ratios; an odds ratio of 1 means no association. Adjust for confounders, but check model assumptions and fit.

sections.heading: Survival and missing data
sections.text: Survival analysis handles time until an event, such as death or recovery. Censoring means the event was not observed before the end of follow-up. Kaplan-Meier curves estimate survival; the log-rank test compares curves; Cox regression gives hazard ratios. Missing data can bias results. MCAR means missing completely at random; MAR means missingness can be explained by observed variables; MNAR means it depends on unobserved values. Complete-case analysis is often biased. Multiple imputation is common for MAR data. Use software such as R, Stata or SPSS, but pre-specify analyses, keep code, and report methods and limitations honestly.

keyPoints: Use independent t-test for two independent means, paired t-test for paired means, ANOVA for three or more means, and chi-square for categorical association.
Report effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals; a p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Pearson and Spearman correlation measure association; correlation does not prove causation.
Linear regression: y = a + bx; logistic regression reports odds ratios.
Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox models handle time-to-event data with censoring.
Missing data may be MCAR, MAR or MNAR; multiple imputation is common for MAR but not MNAR.

en.title: Screening and the evaluation of diagnostic tests
en.short: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, bias and screening criteria.

sections.heading: Test accuracy
sections.text: Screening tests people who appear healthy, to find disease early. A test is judged against a reference standard, and results form a 2 × 2 table. Sensitivity is TP/(TP+FN), the proportion with disease who test positive. Specificity is TN/(TN+FP), the proportion without disease who test negative. These are properties of the test at a chosen cut-off. Predictive values depend on prevalence. Positive predictive value (PPV) is TP/(TP+FP); negative predictive value (NPV) is TN/(TN+FN). Likelihood ratios summarise test information: LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity), and LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity. LR+ above 1 raises the probability of disease; LR− below 1 lowers it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take 10,000 people with prevalence 2%. Sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. Diseased: 200; non-diseased: 9,800. True positives = 180, false negatives = 20, false positives = 490, true negatives = 9,310. PPV = 180/(180+490) = 26.9%. NPV = 9,310/(9,310+20) = 99.8%. LR+ = 0.90/0.05 = 18; LR− = 0.10/0.95 = 0.105. If prevalence is 10%, PPV = 900/(900+450) = 66.7%, while NPV is 98.8%. Prevalence changes predictive values, not sensitivity or specificity.

sections.heading: Reliability and bias
sections.text: Reliability is repeatability: the same test gives consistent results on repetition. Validity is whether the test measures what it claims to measure. Screening programmes also face bias. Lead-time bias means earlier diagnosis appears to lengthen survival even when death occurs at the same age. Length bias means screening detects slow-growing disease more often than fast-growing disease, making screened cases look milder. Overdiagnosis is detection of disease that would never have caused harm.

sections.heading: Screening criteria
sections.text: Wilson and Jungner set out principles for screening programmes for the World Health Organization in 1968. The condition should be an important health problem. There should be an accepted treatment, facilities for diagnosis and treatment, a latent stage, a suitable test, and an agreed policy on whom to treat. The cost should be acceptable, and case finding should be continuous. These criteria remind us that screening is a programme, not just a test, and can cause harm.

keyPoints: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN); specificity = TN/(TN+FP); both are properties of the test at a chosen cut-off.
PPV = TP/(TP+FP) and NPV = TN/(TN+FN); predictive values change with prevalence.
LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.
Reliability is repeatability; validity is whether a test measures what it claims.
Lead-time bias and length bias can make screening look better than it is.
Wilson and Jungner criteria require an important problem, accepted treatment, suitable test, agreed policy and acceptable cost.

en.title: Communicable disease control
en.short: Malaria, TB, HIV, neglected tropical diseases and zoonoses: case finding, adherence, vectors and One Health.

sections.heading: Control aims
sections.text: Communicable diseases spread from person to person, from animals, or through vectors, food, water and air. Control means reducing transmission and harm to a level the health system can manage; it does not necessarily remove the infection. Main tools include case finding, treatment, adherence support, contact tracing, vector control, vaccination and safe water and hygiene. For malaria, control combines prompt diagnosis and treatment with insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying. For tuberculosis and HIV, early diagnosis and sustained treatment are central. Clinical choices follow national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Finding and following cases
sections.text: Case finding means actively looking for people with infection, for example screening household contacts of a tuberculosis patient or offering HIV testing. Contact tracing finds people exposed to an infectious case so they can be tested, treated or monitored. Treatment adherence means taking treatment as prescribed for as long as needed. Support may include counselling, reminders, community distributors and transport help. Poor adherence can cause treatment failure and, in tuberculosis, drug resistance. Programmes use directly observed or supported treatment according to local policy.

sections.heading: Vectors, animals and One Health
sections.text: Vector control reduces the insects or animals that carry infection. For malaria this includes nets and spraying; for some neglected tropical diseases it includes snail or tsetse control. Neglected tropical diseases are a group of infections that mainly affect poor communities, such as lymphatic filariasis, schistosomiasis and trachoma. Zoonoses are diseases that pass from animals to people, such as rabies and brucellosis. One Health is an approach in which human, animal and environmental health workers plan together.

sections.heading: Elimination and eradication
sections.text: Elimination means reducing cases in a defined area to zero, while keeping measures to prevent return. Eradication means permanent global reduction to zero, so no measures are needed. Smallpox was eradicated; polio is close but not yet certified. A district may eliminate malaria locally while global transmission continues. In a village, a tuberculosis case is found, contacts are traced and tested, and a community worker supports adherence. This breaks transmission and prevents resistance.

keyPoints: Control reduces transmission and harm; elimination and eradication are stricter goals.
Case finding and contact tracing find infection early and link people to care.
Adherence support is essential to cure and to prevent drug resistance.
Vector control and safe water and hygiene reduce transmission of many communicable diseases.
One Health links human, animal and environmental health for zoonoses.
Clinical decisions should follow current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Immunisation programmes
en.short: National schedules, cold chain, coverage and safety monitoring, and reaching under-immunised children.

sections.heading: Schedules and variation
sections.text: A national immunisation schedule states which vaccines are offered, at what age, and how many doses. It is set by the national immunisation technical advisory group and ministry of health, using disease burden, vaccine safety and efficacy, cost, supply, and health system capacity. WHO provides global recommendations, but countries adapt them. Schedules therefore differ: some add vaccines for local diseases, use different products, or start at different ages. Always check the current national schedule and WHO guidance; they change.

sections.heading: Cold chain and storage
sections.text: The cold chain is the system that keeps vaccines within the temperature range set by the manufacturer and national guidance from manufacture to use. Many routine vaccines need +2 to +8°C, and some must not freeze. It includes refrigerators, cold boxes, temperature monitors, vaccine vial monitors, trained staff, and contingency plans. A break can reduce vaccine potency without visible change. Record temperatures, act on alarms, and follow national guidance on storage, transport and disposal.

sections.heading: Coverage and safety
sections.text: Coverage is the proportion of the target population that has received a vaccine dose. Administrative coverage divides doses given by the estimated target population; it can be wrong if denominators or reports are poor. Surveys give a check. For example, if 380 of 400 sampled children received a third DTP-containing dose, coverage is 380 ÷ 400 × 100 = 95%. High coverage also protects the wider community through herd immunity. Monitor adverse events following immunisation (AEFI), report them promptly, and assess causality through national systems. AEFI monitoring protects trust and detects problems.

sections.heading: Reaching under-immunised
sections.text: Under-immunised children include zero-dose children, who have missed routine vaccines, and those with incomplete doses. Strategies include microplanning (detailed local planning) with local data, outreach and mobile teams, defaulter tracing (finding children who missed doses), reminder systems, integrating immunisation with other services, and community engagement to address hesitancy and access barriers. Focus on remote rural areas, urban slums and conflict settings. Use current WHO and national guidance for catch-up schedules and programme reviews.

keyPoints: National schedules are set nationally using local disease burden, vaccine characteristics, cost and system capacity, so they differ between countries.
The cold chain keeps vaccines within the temperature range set by the manufacturer and national guidance; many routine vaccines need +2 to +8°C and some must not freeze.
Administrative coverage = doses given ÷ estimated target population × 100; survey coverage helps check it.
AEFI means adverse event following immunisation; report events promptly and use national causality assessment systems.
Reach under-immunised children through microplanning, outreach, defaulter tracing, reminders, service integration and community engagement.
Check current WHO and national guidance, because schedules, storage rules and reporting systems change.

en.title: Maternal, newborn and child health
en.short: Causes of maternal, newborn and child death and proven care from pregnancy to childhood.

sections.heading: Causes and continuum
sections.text: Maternal, newborn and child health covers the health of women during pregnancy and after birth, of babies in the first 28 days, and of children through adolescence. The main causes of maternal death are severe bleeding, hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia, infection, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion. Newborn deaths are mainly from preterm birth, complications around birth and infection. Child deaths are mainly from pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria, malnutrition and newborn conditions. Most are preventable through proven care along a continuum: adolescence, pregnancy, birth, the postnatal period and childhood.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and birth
sections.text: Antenatal care means scheduled contacts during pregnancy to assess risk, treat problems and give information. It works best when linked to skilled birth attendance: care at birth by a trained health worker, such as a midwife or doctor, who can manage normal birth and refer complications. Emergency obstetric and newborn care provides surgery, blood and newborn resuscitation when needed. Immediate newborn care includes drying, warmth, early breastfeeding and clean cord care. Kangaroo mother care, skin-to-skin contact with frequent breastfeeding, helps small and preterm babies. A case: Amina, 17, attends antenatal care, is found to have high blood pressure and is referred; skilled care at birth can prevent eclampsia.

sections.heading: Childhood, adolescents and family planning
sections.text: After birth, postnatal care checks the mother and baby for danger signs and supports breastfeeding and family planning. Child health includes growth monitoring: regular measurement of weight and height plotted on a growth chart to detect faltering growth, with counselling and referral. Proven child interventions include immunisation, oral rehydration salts and zinc for diarrhoea, antibiotics for pneumonia, malaria prevention and treatment, and vitamin A. Family planning helps people choose the number and timing of pregnancies and reduces risks from too early, too close or too many births. Adolescent health needs confidential services, information and support to stay in school. Guidelines change; check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

keyPoints: Most maternal, newborn and child deaths are preventable through proven care along the continuum.
Maternal deaths are mainly from severe bleeding, hypertensive disorders, infection, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion.
Newborn deaths are mainly from preterm birth, complications around birth and infection.
Skilled birth attendance and emergency obstetric and newborn care are central to safe birth.
Growth monitoring means regular weight and height measurement plotted on a growth chart to detect faltering growth.
Family planning and adolescent health reduce risks from early, close or many pregnancies; check current national or World Health Organization guidance.

en.title: Nutrition and food safety
en.short: Nutrient needs, malnutrition, fortification, supplementation and food safety systems.

sections.heading: Nutrient needs
sections.text: Macronutrients (protein, carbohydrate and fat) supply energy and building blocks. Micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are needed in small amounts. Needs differ with age, sex, pregnancy, lactation, activity and illness. Dietary reference values are set nationally or by WHO and FAO, and they change, so check current tables. Energy can be estimated with Atwater factors: protein 4 kcal/g, carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, fat 9 kcal/g. For example, 100 g of a food with 10 g protein, 20 g carbohydrate and 5 g fat gives (10×4)+(20×4)+(5×9)=40+80+45=165 kcal.

sections.heading: Malnutrition
sections.text: Undernutrition includes stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height), underweight (low weight for age) and micronutrient deficiencies. Overnutrition means overweight and obesity, which raise the risk of diabetes, heart disease and some cancers. Many countries face a double burden: undernutrition and obesity in the same community or household. Causes include not only food shortage but also infection, poor care, unsafe water and poverty.

sections.heading: Fortification and supplementation
sections.text: Fortification adds micronutrients to commonly eaten foods, such as iodised salt or vitamin A in cooking oil; it reaches many people without changing diets. Supplementation gives a concentrated dose to people at high risk, such as vitamin A capsules or iron and folic acid in pregnancy. Both need regulation, quality control and monitoring. Doses and schedules differ by country; follow current national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Food safety
sections.text: Food-borne disease comes from bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins and chemicals in food or water. Hygiene means clean hands, safe water, separating raw and cooked food, thorough cooking, safe storage and pest control. A national food safety system uses risk analysis: risk assessment, management and communication. It includes laws and standards, inspection, laboratory testing, outbreak surveillance and traceability. HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) is a preventive system that identifies hazards and controls them at critical points.

keyPoints: Macronutrients supply energy; protein and carbohydrate give about 4 kcal/g and fat about 9 kcal/g.
Dietary reference values vary by country and life stage; check current WHO or national tables.
Undernutrition includes stunting and wasting; overnutrition includes overweight and obesity.
Fortification adds nutrients to common foods; supplementation gives concentrated doses to high-risk groups.
Food hygiene prevents food-borne disease through clean hands, safe water, cooking and separation of raw and cooked food.
A national food safety system uses risk analysis, standards, inspection, surveillance and HACCP.

en.title: Noncommunicable diseases: burden, shared risks and prevention
en.short: Burden and shared risks of NCDs, WHO best buys, tobacco, alcohol, diet, inactivity and injury prevention.

sections.heading: What NCDs are
sections.text: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), also called chronic diseases, are not passed from person to person. The main four are cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer and chronic lung disease. They cause a large share of deaths worldwide, including in low- and middle-income countries. The burden includes premature death, disability and high costs. Many NCDs share modifiable risk factors, meaning risks people can change: tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity. These risks often begin early and cluster in the same people and communities.

sections.heading: Shared risk factors
sections.text: Tobacco, smoked or smokeless, raises the risk of heart disease, cancer and lung disease. Harmful alcohol use raises the risk of liver disease, several cancers and injuries. An unhealthy diet is high in salt, sugar and saturated fat and low in fruit and vegetables. Physical inactivity adds independent risk. A 55-year-old teacher who smokes, drinks heavily, eats processed food and walks little has several risks acting together, so his risk is higher than with one risk alone. Population prevention aims to shift the whole distribution of risk, not only to advise high-risk individuals.

sections.heading: WHO best buys
sections.text: WHO identifies cost-effective population measures, often called best buys, that countries can adapt. For tobacco: raise taxes, make public places smoke-free, require health warnings and ban advertising. For alcohol: raise taxes, restrict availability and marketing, and enforce drink-driving laws. For diet: reformulate foods, label packages, restrict marketing to children and use fiscal measures. For physical activity: public education and planning that supports walking and cycling. Health-system measures include screening, treatment and vaccines such as HPV and hepatitis B. National policy differs, so check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Preventing injuries
sections.text: Injuries are not random accidents. Road traffic crashes, falls, burns, drowning, poisoning and violence follow patterns and can be prevented. Measures include speed limits, helmet and seat-belt laws, child restraints, safer roads, safe storage of poisons, and enforcement. Surveillance shows where injuries happen, and first aid and emergency care reduce harm. Prevention combines education, engineering and legislation.

keyPoints: NCDs are chronic, non-infectious diseases; the main four are cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer and chronic lung disease.
Tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity are shared modifiable risk factors that often cluster.
WHO best buys are cost-effective population measures such as taxes, smoke-free laws, advertising bans, labelling and restrictions on alcohol availability and marketing.
Health-system actions include screening, treatment and vaccines such as HPV and hepatitis B, adapted to national guidance.
Injuries are preventable, not random accidents; road safety laws, safer environments, surveillance and emergency care reduce harm.
Prevention should combine population measures with support for high-risk individuals, and policies must be enforced and evaluated.

en.title: Occupational health and safety
en.short: Hazards, occupational disease, risk assessment, controls, health services and labour law.

sections.heading: Hazards and exposure
sections.text: An occupational hazard is anything at work that can harm health. Physical hazards include noise, vibration, heat and radiation. Chemical hazards include solvents, dusts and pesticides; harm depends on concentration, duration and route, by inhalation or skin contact. Biological hazards include bacteria, viruses and needlestick injuries. Ergonomic hazards are poor work design, such as awkward posture or heavy lifting. Psychosocial hazards include long hours, low control, harassment and job insecurity. Hazard is not risk: risk is the chance and seriousness of harm.

sections.heading: Occupational disease
sections.text: Occupational diseases are illnesses caused mainly by work exposures. Examples are noise-induced hearing loss, silicosis from silica dust, occupational asthma, contact dermatitis, lead poisoning, musculoskeletal disorders and work-related stress. Recognition needs an occupational history: jobs, tasks, exposures, duration, protection and timing of symptoms. Symptoms that improve away from work suggest a work link. Report suspected cases under national rules; reporting schemes differ.

sections.heading: Risk assessment and controls
sections.text: Risk assessment is a structured check: identify hazards, decide who may be harmed and how, evaluate risk, record and review. Controls follow a hierarchy. First eliminate the hazard, then substitute something safer, then use engineering controls such as ventilation or machine guards. Administrative controls, such as training and safe procedures, come next. Personal protective equipment (PPE) is the last line and depends on correct fit and use. For example, a solvent factory can enclose the process and extract fumes; respirators are added only if exposure remains.

sections.heading: Services and labour law
sections.text: Occupational health services advise on fitness for work, health surveillance, vaccination and return to work. They do not replace safety controls. Labour law sets duties on employers and workers. Rules differ by country: the UK has the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, the US the Occupational Safety and Health Act 1970, South Africa the Occupational Health and Safety Act 1993, and Nigeria the Factories Act and Employees’ Compensation Act 2010. ILO sets international standards. Check national law and WHO or ILO guidance; this is not medical advice.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance and seriousness of harm from it.
The main hazard groups are physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic and psychosocial.
Occupational disease recognition depends on a detailed job and exposure history.
Controls follow the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, then PPE.
PPE is the last line of defence and needs correct fit and use.
Labour law and occupational health services differ by country; check current national and ILO or WHO guidance.

en.title: Water, sanitation and hygiene
en.short: Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene: disease routes, water safety, sanitation options and promotion.

sections.heading: Disease routes
sections.text: WASH means water, sanitation and hygiene. Unsafe water, poor sanitation and unhygienic behaviour cause diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A and E, polio and soil-transmitted helminths. Transmission is mainly faecal-oral: pathogens leave faeces and reach the mouth through water, food, hands, flies or soil. Water-related diseases are often grouped as waterborne (drinking contaminated water), water-washed (diseases reduced by more water for washing, such as trachoma), water-based (a parasite with a water-living stage, such as schistosomiasis) and vector-borne (insects breeding in water).

sections.heading: Water safety
sections.text: Safe water needs source protection, treatment and safe storage. Treatment usually combines sedimentation, filtration and disinfection; chlorination leaves a residual that protects water after treatment. Boiling and solar disinfection are household options, but they need correct use. Testing uses faecal indicator bacteria such as E. coli, plus turbidity (cloudiness) and chlorine residual, and a sanitary inspection of the source and storage. A single test shows conditions at that moment, not permanent safety. Follow current WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality and national standards.

sections.heading: Sanitation and waste
sections.text: Sanitation separates excreta from people. Improved options include pour-flush latrines, septic tanks and sewers, but they work only if used and maintained. On-site systems produce faecal sludge, which must be emptied, transported and treated safely. Safe waste management also covers solid waste and health-care waste, because uncontrolled dumping attracts flies and other disease carriers and pollutes water. Sanitation programmes need demand creation, affordable services and attention to the whole chain from toilet to final treatment.

sections.heading: Hygiene and example
sections.text: Hygiene promotion enables handwashing with soap at critical times, food hygiene and safe water handling. It works better with facilities, social norms and community participation than with messages alone. Example: Amina’s household in northern Nigeria shares an unprotected well. A community worker arranges safe storage, chlorination and latrines, and promotes handwashing after toilet use and before food. Diarrhoea falls when all parts improve together. Check current national guidance.

keyPoints: Most WASH-related infections spread by the faecal-oral route.
Waterborne, water-washed, water-based and vector-borne describe different links to water.
Safe water depends on source protection, treatment and safe storage.
Faecal indicator testing and sanitary inspection assess water safety, but a test is only a snapshot.
Sanitation must cover the whole chain, including safe faecal sludge treatment.
Hygiene promotion works best with facilities, social norms and community participation, not messages alone.

en.title: Health policy, planning and management
en.short: The policy cycle, stakeholders, priority setting, planning models, stewardship, regulation and decentralisation.

sections.heading: Policy cycle and priorities
sections.text: Public policy is a course of action chosen by government. The policy cycle is a model with stages: agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation. Real policy is messier, with loops and politics. Stakeholder analysis identifies the people and groups affected by or able to influence a policy, and maps their interests, power and position. Priority setting means choosing what to fund when resources are limited. Common criteria are burden of disease, cost-effectiveness, equity, feasibility and political support. In a district planning meeting in northern Nigeria, Amina’s team compares expanding antenatal clinics with buying a new ambulance. They score each option on those criteria. The clinics score higher on equity and cost per person reached, so they are funded first.

sections.heading: Planning models and stewardship
sections.text: Health planning models include comprehensive rational planning, which sets objectives, assesses needs, chooses priorities and evaluates; incremental planning, which adjusts the current budget in small steps; and participatory planning, which involves communities and front-line staff. Stewardship is government’s overall responsibility for the health system: setting direction, gathering intelligence and regulating. Regulation uses rules, licensing and accreditation to control quality, safety and prices. Human resources for health planning matches the number, skills and distribution of staff to need, and addresses shortages and rural imbalance.

sections.heading: Decentralisation and governance
sections.text: Decentralisation moves authority and resources from central government to local bodies. It can improve responsiveness and local ownership, but may fragment services, weaken accountability or widen inequity if local capacity and funding are weak. Governance is how decisions are made and checked. Good governance means transparency, clear roles, community voice and action against corruption. These choices affect service delivery: a clinic may have staff and drugs on paper, but poor governance or delayed funds can leave patients untreated. Policy, planning and management therefore link political choices to the everyday working of health services.

keyPoints: The policy cycle has agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation, but real policy is not linear.
Stakeholder analysis maps the interests, power and position of groups affected by a policy.
Priority setting uses explicit criteria such as burden of disease, cost-effectiveness, equity and feasibility.
Main planning models are comprehensive rational, incremental and participatory.
Stewardship is government’s steering role: direction, intelligence and regulation.
Decentralisation can improve responsiveness but risks fragmentation and inequity when local capacity is weak.

en.title: Health economics and health financing
en.short: Demand, supply, market failure, cost-effectiveness, financing mechanisms and universal health coverage.

sections.heading: Demand, supply, failure
sections.text: Demand is willingness and ability to pay for care; need is capacity to benefit. Price, income and insurance affect demand. Supply depends on staff, facilities, medicines, technology and budgets. Health care is not a typical market. Patients lack information, providers know more, and insurance changes behaviour. Vaccination protects others, an externality, and surveillance is close to a public good. Insurers face adverse selection when sicker people buy cover, and moral hazard when cover raises use. These market failures justify public action and make equity a goal.

sections.heading: Cost and evaluation
sections.text: Costs include fixed costs, which do not change with output, and variable costs, which do. Average cost is total cost divided by output; marginal cost is the cost of one more unit. Cost-effectiveness analysis compares cost with a health outcome, often cost per DALY averted, where one DALY is one lost healthy year. Cost-benefit analysis values benefits in money. Example: intervention A costs USD 200,000 and averts 100 DALYs, so USD 2,000 per DALY. Intervention B costs USD 150,000 and averts 50 DALYs, so USD 3,000 per DALY. A is more cost-effective.

sections.heading: Financing and coverage
sections.text: Financing mechanisms are tax revenue, social health insurance, private voluntary insurance, out-of-pocket payments and donor funds. Tax funding pools government revenue; social insurance pools mandatory contributions, often linked to employment; private insurance pools voluntary premiums. Out-of-pocket payment at the point of use is least protective: it can deter care and cause financial hardship. Donor funds can help but may be fragmented and time-limited. Financial risk protection means prepayment and pooling spread the cost of illness. Equity means fair distribution: horizontal equity treats equals equally; vertical equity treats people according to need or ability to pay. Universal health coverage means all people receive needed services without financial hardship, not free care. Countries progress by increasing prepaid pooled funds, defining a benefit package, strengthening primary care and reducing out-of-pocket payment. Check national and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Demand reflects willingness and ability to pay; need reflects capacity to benefit.
Health care markets fail because of information asymmetry, externalities, public goods and insurance problems such as adverse selection and moral hazard.
Cost-effectiveness ratio = cost ÷ health gain; cost-benefit analysis values benefits in money.
In the example, USD 200,000 for 100 DALYs averted is USD 2,000 per DALY, cheaper than USD 3,000 per DALY.
Financial risk protection comes from prepayment and pooling, not from out-of-pocket payment at the point of use.
Universal health coverage means needed services without financial hardship, and countries reach it by increasing pooled prepaid funds and reducing out-of-pocket payment.

en.title: Public health ethics and law
en.short: Ethical tensions, quarantine powers, privacy and consent in population health law.

sections.heading: Ethical tensions
sections.text: Public health ethics asks how to protect populations while respecting persons. Individual liberty can conflict with collective protection: a measure may limit movement or choice to reduce harm to others. Paternalism is acting for people’s good against their wishes. It needs strong justification: serious harm, good evidence, proportionality and the least restrictive option. Equity means fair treatment, not identical treatment; resources should go where need is greatest. Stigma is a mark of disgrace that can make people hide symptoms or avoid services. Privacy and confidentiality protect personal information and trust.

sections.heading: Law and disease control
sections.text: Public health law gives officials duties and powers, and limits them. Quarantine restricts people who were exposed but are not yet ill. Isolation separates people who are ill. Statutes differ by country. England has the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984; the United States relies heavily on state police powers; Nigeria has a Quarantine Act and state public health laws; South Africa’s National Health Act 61 of 2003 provides a framework. Some laws allow a health officer to order detention; others require a court. Rules should be lawful, necessary, proportionate, time-limited and open to review. Check current national law and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Data, consent and case
sections.text: Data protection law governs personal health data. Consent is one lawful basis, but public health laws may permit processing without consent when necessary and safeguarded. Collect the minimum data, keep it secure, and share only with those who need it. Examples include the EU GDPR, the UK Data Protection Act 2018, Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and South Africa’s POPIA. In a case, a district officer learns that a market trader has infectious tuberculosis. The officer wants to warn the trader’s customers. Ethics asks whether warning is necessary and proportionate or mainly stigmatising. Law sets when notification to the health authority is required and when wider disclosure is allowed. The trader should be told, supported and involved; share the least information needed.

keyPoints: Public health ethics balances collective protection with individual liberty, equity and privacy.
Paternalism needs serious harm, evidence, proportionality and the least restrictive option.
Quarantine restricts exposed people; isolation separates ill people.
Public health statutes differ by country and may require a court order or allow a health officer to act.
Data protection requires minimum data, security and need-to-know sharing; consent is not the only lawful basis.
Stigma can undermine surveillance and care, so disclosure should be necessary and proportionate.

en.title: Health information systems and monitoring and evaluation
en.short: Routine health information systems, data quality, monitoring and evaluation, indicators and using data.

sections.heading: Routine systems
sections.text: A routine health information system (RHIS) collects data as services are delivered: attendance, diagnoses, treatments and stock use. It differs from surveys and surveillance, which answer specific or outbreak questions. RHIS data are usually collected by facility staff in registers and sent upward monthly. The system should be simple, standardised and linked to local decisions. If staff see no use for the data, reporting becomes a burden and quality falls.

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Data quality has several dimensions: completeness, timeliness, accuracy, consistency and validity. Completeness is the share of expected reports received. If 36 of 40 facilities report, completeness is 36 ÷ 40 × 100 = 90%. Accuracy means the report matches the register. Consistency means the same figure agrees across sources. Data quality audits compare registers, reports and summaries, then give feedback. Good quality needs clear definitions, training and checks, not blame.

sections.heading: Monitoring and evaluation
sections.text: Monitoring is continuous, routine tracking of activities against plans. Evaluation is a periodic, structured judgement of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability. A logical framework links inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact, and states assumptions. An indicator is a variable that measures change; a target is the level expected by a stated date. For example, a target may be 80% of reports submitted on time. Monitoring compares monthly performance with that target. Evaluation asks whether the system improved decisions and health outcomes.

sections.heading: Process, outcome and use
sections.text: Process evaluation asks whether activities were delivered as planned: training held, registers used, reports sent. Outcome evaluation asks whether results changed: data reviewed in meetings, coverage or service quality. Data support decisions only when they are reviewed, interpreted and acted on. A district team might find 90% completeness but late reports from remote clinics. It could ask why, then adjust the deadline or send reminders. This feedback loop is data for decision-making. Country platforms and reporting rules vary, so check current national guidance.

keyPoints: A routine health information system collects service data continuously; surveys and surveillance answer specific questions.
Data quality covers completeness, timeliness, accuracy, consistency and validity.
Completeness = reports received ÷ expected reports × 100; 36 of 40 gives 90%.
Monitoring tracks plans continuously; evaluation judges results periodically.
A logical framework links inputs to impact; indicators measure change and targets set expected levels.
Process evaluation checks delivery; outcome evaluation checks results; data must be reviewed and acted on.

en.title: Community diagnosis and community engagement
