en.short: Community entry, participatory needs assessment, mobilisation and working with health workers and leaders.

sections.heading: Entry and diagnosis
sections.text: Community entry is the planned process of gaining permission and trust before asking people for information. Start with local government and facility leaders, then meet recognised community leaders. Explain the purpose, who will see the data and what the community gains. Community diagnosis is a systematic description of a defined community’s health needs, resources and priorities. It combines existing records with local knowledge. Participatory needs assessment means community members help decide what to ask and how to interpret answers. Useful methods include mapping, transect walks (walking a fixed route through the community to observe conditions), focus group discussions and key informant interviews. Triangulate: compare several sources before calling a finding. Seek informed consent, protect privacy and feed results back.

sections.heading: Partners and mobilisation
sections.text: Community health workers are local people trained to provide basic services and link households to facilities. Their role, training and supervision differ by country, so follow national policy. Traditional and religious leaders can open doors, correct rumours and support uptake, but they are not a single voice. Map stakeholders, including women’s groups, youth groups and civil society organisations, which are non-state groups such as associations and NGOs. Community mobilisation is the process of bringing people together to act on a shared problem. Social marketing uses commercial methods to promote healthy behaviour or products, with careful attention to ethics and affordability.

sections.heading: Case and principles
sections.text: In a Nigerian town, a primary health centre wanted to improve antenatal attendance. The team met the ward councillor, the traditional ruler and the imam, then held separate meetings with women’s groups. A participatory assessment found that women feared long waits and rude staff, not only distance. The centre changed appointment times, trained staff in respectful care and asked a civil society group to help monitor. Attendance was reviewed monthly with the community. Principles: work with existing structures, share power, avoid raising expectations you cannot meet, and check current national guidance.

keyPoints: Community entry earns permission and trust before data collection.
Community diagnosis describes needs, resources and priorities using several sources.
Participatory needs assessment involves community members in choosing questions and interpreting findings.
Community health workers, traditional and religious leaders, and civil society can support engagement, but their roles vary by country.
Community mobilisation brings people together to act; social marketing applies commercial methods ethically to health behaviour.
Feed findings back and check current national guidance before acting.

en.title: Emergency preparedness and global health
en.short: Disaster and epidemic preparedness, incident command, risk communication, health clusters and global health governance.

sections.heading: Preparedness
sections.text:
Emergency preparedness means the plans, capacities and resources needed to respond to disasters and epidemics. It starts with risk assessment: identify hazards, who is exposed and vulnerable, and what capacities exist. Preparedness is often organised as an all-hazards cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. Epidemic preparedness adds surveillance, laboratory access, stockpiles, trained staff, emergency operations centres and exercises.

Plans must be tested through drills and updated after every response. Preparedness also needs water, transport, communication and community groups.

sections.heading: Command and coordination
sections.text:
An incident command system is a management structure for emergencies. It gives one incident commander clear authority and divides work into operations, planning, logistics and finance or administration. It began in the United States; forms vary by country. It helps teams speak through one chain of command.

In humanitarian emergencies, the cluster approach groups agencies by sector. The Health Cluster, led globally by WHO, coordinates health partners with the ministry of health to reduce gaps and duplication. Clusters are used in some responses, not every outbreak.

sections.heading: Risk communication
sections.text:
Risk communication is the real-time exchange of information, advice and opinions between officials and people facing a threat. It is not one-way public relations. Good practice is timely, transparent, consistent and based on listening to communities.

Officials should say what is known, what is uncertain and what people can do, without overpromising. Trust is built before an emergency through community engagement. In an outbreak, messages should use local languages and trusted messengers to counter rumours.

sections.heading: Governance and displacement
sections.text:
Global health governance is the institutions, rules and processes that shape responses to health threats. WHO sets norms, gives technical guidance and coordinates under the International Health Regulations, a binding agreement among member states. National agencies, such as ministries of health, lead within their countries.

Conflict and displacement cause injury, infectious disease, malnutrition, mental distress and interrupted care. In a Nigerian flooding case, Dr Adebayo activates the emergency operations centre. Ms Ngozi’s team sends radio messages, while partners map gaps.

keyPoints: Emergency preparedness uses an all-hazards cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.
An incident command system gives one commander clear authority and divides work into operations, planning, logistics and finance or administration.
Risk communication is timely, transparent, two-way exchange with affected communities, not one-way public relations.
In some humanitarian emergencies, the Health Cluster, led globally by WHO, coordinates health partners with national authorities.
WHO sets norms and gives guidance under the International Health Regulations, while national agencies lead within their countries.
Conflict and displacement raise risks of injury, infectious disease, malnutrition, mental distress and interrupted care.

en.title: Advanced epidemiological methods and causal inference
en.short: Covers DAGs, confounding, collider bias, mediation, propensity scores, IVs and Mendelian randomisation.

sections.heading: Causal diagrams
sections.text: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a diagram of variables and arrows that encodes causal assumptions. Arrows show direct effects, and no arrow means no direct effect is assumed. A DAG helps choose which variables to adjust for and which to leave alone. It is a tool for reasoning, not proof of causation. Draw the graph before analysis and state the assumptions plainly.

sections.heading: Confounding and colliders
sections.text: A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome. It creates a non-causal association. A collider is a common effect of two variables. Adjusting for a collider can create bias, called collider bias, even when no confounding exists. Example: 200 exposed and 200 unexposed people. Crude risk is 40/200 = 20% versus 30/200 = 15%, so RR = 20/15 = 1.33. Stratify by age. Younger: 10/100 = 10% versus 15/150 = 10%. Older: 30/100 = 30% versus 15/50 = 30%. Both stratum RRs are 1.0, so age confounded the crude result.

sections.heading: Effect modification and mediation
sections.text: Effect modification means the exposure effect differs across levels of another variable, such as age. It is not confounding; report the separate effects. Mediation means part of the effect passes through an intermediate variable. The total effect can be split into direct and indirect effects, but this needs strong assumptions. Do not adjust for a mediator if you want the total effect.

sections.heading: Methods and appraisal
sections.text: Propensity scores give each person the estimated probability of exposure given covariates: e(X) = P(T = 1 | X). They can balance groups but cannot remove unmeasured confounding. Instrumental variables affect exposure but not outcome except through exposure; they need relevance, exclusion and independence, meaning there is no common cause of the instrument and the outcome. Mendelian randomisation uses genetic variants as instruments. Critical appraisal asks whether the DAG is credible, whether selection and measurement were sound, and whether sensitivity analyses were reported.

keyPoints: A DAG encodes causal assumptions and guides adjustment; it does not prove causation.
A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome; a collider is a common effect, and adjusting for a collider can create bias.
Crude risk ratio = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; in the example 20% ÷ 15% = 1.33, while age-specific RRs were 1.0.
Effect modification means the effect differs by stratum; mediation means part of the effect runs through an intermediate variable.
Propensity score e(X) = P(T = 1 | X) balances measured covariates but cannot control unmeasured confounding.
Instrumental variables and Mendelian randomisation need relevance, exclusion and independence assumptions, and critical appraisal should test these assumptions and sensitivity analyses.

en.title: Implementation science and programme evaluation
en.short: Frameworks, fidelity, scale-up and process, outcome and economic evaluation of health programmes.

sections.heading: Frameworks and context
sections.text: Implementation science studies how to move evidence-based interventions into routine practice. RE-AIM assesses Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation and Maintenance. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) organises barriers and facilitators across the intervention, outer setting, inner setting, individuals and process. Barriers may include cost, staff workload and weak leadership; facilitators may include training, supportive supervision and community trust. Context matters: an intervention that works in one district may fail elsewhere.

sections.heading: Fidelity and scale-up
sections.text: Fidelity is the degree to which an intervention is delivered as intended: content, dose and quality. Adaptation is a deliberate change to fit local needs. Record adaptations and keep core components intact, or the programme may drift. Scale-up means expanding an effective intervention under routine conditions. It needs financing, workforce, governance and monitoring, not just a good trial result.

sections.heading: Evaluation designs
sections.text: Process evaluation checks reach, dose, fidelity and acceptability. Outcome evaluation measures intended changes in health or intermediate outcomes. Economic evaluation compares costs with consequences, using cost-effectiveness, cost-utility or cost-benefit analysis. Randomised designs include individual and cluster trials; stepped-wedge trials roll out an intervention over time. Quasi-experimental designs include interrupted time series, difference-in-differences and propensity scores when randomisation is not feasible. Example: intervention clinic improves coverage from 20% to 30%; control clinic from 25% to 27%. Difference-in-differences = (30 − 20) − (27 − 25) = 10 − 2 = 8 percentage points.

sections.heading: Using findings
sections.text: A logic model links inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact. Choose indicators before data collection, and report effect sizes with uncertainty and context. A good evaluation is planned at the start. Evaluation should inform decisions, not just judge success. Share findings with communities, managers and funders, and use them to adjust delivery.

keyPoints: Implementation science studies how evidence-based interventions are adopted, delivered and sustained in routine practice.
RE-AIM covers Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation and Maintenance; CFIR maps barriers and facilitators across context.
Fidelity is delivery as intended; adaptation is deliberate local change, and core components should be preserved.
Process evaluation checks implementation; outcome evaluation measures effects; economic evaluation compares costs and consequences.
Randomised and quasi-experimental designs estimate programme effects; difference-in-differences = (intervention after − before) − (control after − before).
Scale-up needs financing, workforce, governance and monitoring, and evaluation should guide decisions.

en.title: Planetary health and climate change
en.short: Climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution and land use as health issues, with adaptation and co-benefits.

sections.heading: Planetary health
sections.text: Planetary health studies how human health depends on natural systems and whether societies stay within safe environmental limits. Climate change means long-term shifts in temperature and weather, driven mainly by greenhouse gases from fossil fuels and land clearing. Biodiversity loss is the decline in the variety and abundance of species and ecosystems. Pollution is contamination of air, water or soil. Land use is how land is used, for example farming, deforestation and urban growth. Each is a health issue.

sections.heading: Effects and vulnerability
sections.text: Direct effects include heat stress, flood injuries and illness from wildfire smoke. Indirect effects work through food and water, disease vectors, displacement and livelihoods. Drought can cut harvests and raise food prices. Warmth and standing water can expand mosquito breeding. Biodiversity loss can disturb pollination and increase contact between people, livestock and wildlife. Pollution raises respiratory and cardiovascular risk. Effects interact: a flood may cause injury, displacement and infection together. Vulnerability is the degree to which a person or community is likely to be harmed. It depends on exposure, sensitivity and capacity to cope. A coastal city with poor drainage, crowded housing and weak health services is more vulnerable than a well-resourced city with early warning and evacuation plans.

sections.heading: Adaptation, mitigation and One Health
sections.text: Adaptation means reducing risks, for example heat action plans, flood defences, resilient water supplies and disease surveillance. It must reach the most vulnerable and be planned with communities. Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gas emissions or removing them from the atmosphere. Health co-benefits are the health gains from these actions: cleaner energy cuts air pollution, and walking and cycling raise physical activity. Sustainable health systems cut their own carbon and waste and prepare for shocks. One Health recognises that human, animal and ecosystem health are linked, so surveillance crosses sectors. Suppose Amina, a district health officer in a drought-affected area, sees more malnutrition and mosquito-borne illness. With farmers, veterinarians and water engineers, she maps risks and strengthens surveillance. This is One Health adaptation.

keyPoints: Planetary health links human health to safe environmental limits.
Climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution and land use affect health directly and indirectly.
Vulnerability depends on exposure, sensitivity and capacity to cope.
Adaptation reduces current and unavoidable risks; mitigation cuts emissions.
Mitigation brings health co-benefits, such as cleaner air and more active travel.
One Health links human, animal and ecosystem health, and sustainable health systems reduce their own environmental harm.

en.title: Public health research methods and the dissertation
en.short: Research question, design, sampling, ethics, data analysis and dissertation writing and defence.

sections.heading: From question to design
sections.text:
A research question states exactly what you will answer, for whom and with what outcome. PICO helps for quantitative work: population, intervention or exposure, comparison and outcome. PICo suits qualitative work: population, phenomenon of interest and context.

A literature review is a structured search and critical appraisal of what is already known, ending in a clear gap. Choose a design that can answer the question: cross-sectional for prevalence, cohort or case-control for associations, qualitative for meaning, mixed methods for both.

sections.heading: Sampling and sample size
sections.text:
Sampling is how you select participants from the population you want to study. Probability methods, such as simple random or cluster sampling, allow generalisation; non-probability methods, such as convenience sampling, do not.

Sample size for a proportion uses n = Z² p(1−p)/d². For 95% confidence, Z = 1.96; if p = 0.5 and d = 0.05, n = 1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so 385. Then adjust for design effect and non-response. For qualitative studies, justify sample size by information power, not a formula.

sections.heading: Questionnaire, ethics and data
sections.text:
A questionnaire must be clear, valid and reliable. Validity means it measures what it claims; reliability means it gives consistent results. Translate and pilot it with people like your participants.

Get ethics approval before collecting data. In Nigeria, the National Health Research Ethics Committee (NHREC) and its National Code of Health Research Ethics set requirements; many countries have their own national guidance, and WHO publishes standards. Ethics covers informed consent, confidentiality, minimal risk and fair selection. Manage data with a codebook, cleaning rules, secure storage and a pre-specified analysis plan.

sections.heading: Writing and defending
sections.text:
Write the dissertation in a clear structure, usually introduction, methods, results and discussion, with limitations and references.

The defence, or viva, is an oral examination. Be ready to explain why you chose the question, design, sample and analysis, and to admit limitations honestly. Check your university’s current regulations for format, word count and submission dates.

keyPoints: A good research question is focused, answerable and states the population, exposure or intervention, comparison and outcome.
A literature review is a structured search and critical appraisal that ends in a clear gap.
The design must match the question; sampling method determines how far results can be generalised.
For a proportion, n = Z² p(1−p)/d²; with 95% confidence, p = 0.5 and d = 0.05, n = 385 before adjusting for design effect and non-response.
Get ethics approval before data collection; in Nigeria follow NHREC and the National Code of Health Research Ethics, and check your own country’s guidance.
Keep a codebook, clean and store data securely, analyse according to a pre-specified plan, and defend your choices honestly.
